reasons: The connection tests are not visible.

terms.meaning: a plain text file holding settings such as keys, kept apart from the code
a doorway other programs use to ask a service for data or answers
a library that loads the settings in a .env file into the program

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and script description
sections.what: Brings in the basic system and path tools and describes the script's purpose. Nothing runs here.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: test_env_loading
sections.title: Environment file check
sections.what: Checks that a .env file exists in the current folder, loads it, and reports the result. Returns true only if loading works.
sections.why: Likely reason: the app needs these settings before anything else can be tested. Reason not stated.
sections.watch_out: It confirms the file loads, not that the settings inside it are correct.

sections.name: test_openai_api (part 1)
sections.title: OpenAI key and connection test
sections.what: Checks that an OpenAI key exists in the settings and starts with the expected prefix. Then calls OpenAI to list models and to create a test embedding, which is a list of numbers that represents text meaning.
sections.why: Likely reason: a wrong or missing key is a common setup failure, so it is checked first.
sections.watch_out: This makes real calls to OpenAI each time it runs, which can cost a little money, and it prints the first 20 characters of the key.

sections.name: test_openai_api (part 2)
sections.title: Test chat model reply
sections.what: Sends one short test message to a chat model and reports whether it answered. Returns true on success. On any error, prints likely causes and returns false.
sections.why: Likely reason: a real reply proves the key, billing and model name all work, which a model list alone does not prove.
sections.watch_out: When the configured model is a GPT-4 model, the test uses GPT-3.5 instead, so a passing test does not prove the main model works.

sections.name: test_sharepoint_config
sections.title: SharePoint settings check
sections.what: Checks the SharePoint settings. If none are set, it reports SharePoint as optional and skips it. If app-only login settings are present, it tries to log in and read the site title. Returns true, false, or nothing when it cannot test.
sections.why: Likely reason: SharePoint is optional, so missing settings are reported as a note rather than a failure.
sections.watch_out: A failed SharePoint login is shown as FAIL, but it does not change the overall result of the run.

sections.name: test_model_config
sections.title: Model settings report
sections.what: Reads the model and retrieval settings and prints them with a short verdict. It labels the model as recommended, cheaper or custom, and says whether the temperature is 0.3 or lower. It always returns true.
sections.why: Likely reason: it helps the owner spot a poor choice, but it is not meant to block the run.
sections.watch_out: Because it always returns true, a poor model setting never makes the run fail.

sections.name: test_chunking_config
sections.title: Chunk size settings report
sections.what: Reads the chunk size and overlap settings and prints whether they look right. Chunk size is how big each piece of a document is when it is split for search. It always returns true.
sections.why: Likely reason: wrong split sizes can reduce search accuracy, so the file warns about unusual values.
sections.watch_out: Like the model report, it always returns true, so bad values only appear as printed warnings.

sections.name: estimate_costs
sections.title: Rough cost estimate
sections.what: Prints a rough price guide for the chosen model and embeddings, with example totals for indexing 100 documents and handling 20 queries. It does not call any API.
sections.why: Likely reason: it gives the owner a sense of likely spending before they use the system.
sections.watch_out: Prices and totals are typed into the file as of 2024, so they are probably out of date.

sections.name: main (part 1)
sections.title: Run all configuration tests
sections.what: Starts the run with a heading. Stops with an error if the .env file is not found. Then runs the environment load test, the OpenAI test, the SharePoint test, the model test and the chunk test, and collects the results.
sections.why: Likely reason: running every check in one go gives the owner the full picture.
sections.watch_out: The .env file is looked for in the folder the command is run from, so running it from another folder wrongly reports the file as missing.

sections.name: main (part 2)
sections.title: Closing message and exit code
sections.what: Prints either next steps for starting the system or a note to fix problems first. Then exits with code 0 if the two critical checks passed, and 1 if not.
sections.why: Likely reason: the exit code lets other programs tell whether the setup is good.
sections.watch_out: Only the environment load test and the OpenAI test decide pass or fail, so a broken SharePoint or model result does not stop the run.

sections.name: entry point
sections.title: Starts the script when run directly
sections.what: Runs the main function when this file is started directly, and does nothing when another file imports it.
sections.why: Likely reason: this is the usual Python pattern for a file that can be run or imported.

summary: A checker script meant to test the .env settings and API connections. Only its opening and first helper were shown.
purpose: Lets someone confirm their setup is correct before running the app.
why: Stated in the docstring: it tests the .env configuration and API connections.
how: The first helper checks that a .env file exists in the current folder, loads it into the program's settings, and reports the result. The other checks, including API connections, model settings, chunking, cost estimates and the main routine, are in sections not shown.
inputs: The .env file in the current folder, and the settings inside it.
outputs: Printed pass or fail messages. The loading helper returns true or false.
risks: In the visible part, only the presence and loading of the file are checked, not the values inside it. A missing file is reported but does not stop the script. The result is false on failure, so a caller that ignores it can miss the problem.
debug: If the script reports that .env is not found, run it from the folder that contains .env. If loading fails, check the file for typing errors. Read the other sections once they are shown.
